final_answer:
**Answer**

No. As of **August 28, 2026**, I did **not** find good evidence that any one Web search engine is **objectively best for every kind of research question**. That conclusion is consistent with information-retrieval research saying relevance is **multidimensional** and depends on the **user, task, and domain**, and with search-evaluation research saying comparisons must account for **different query intents** and **different result presentations**.  
Sources: https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/widm.1541 , https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-37688-7_9

**Supported fact**

- In worldwide usage for **July 2026**, StatCounter reports **Google 91.31%**, **Bing 4.47%**, and **DuckDuckGo 0.65%** search-engine market share. That shows dominance in use, not universal superiority in all research tasks.  
Source: https://gs.statcounter.com/search-engine-market-share

- DuckDuckGo says it maintains **DuckDuckBot** and “many indexes,” but its “traditional links and images” are **largely sourced from Bing**.  
Source: https://duckduckgo.com/duckduckgo-help-pages/results/sources

- Brave says Brave Search is powered by a **“completely independent index of the Web”** and fetches **millions of webpages every day**. This is a **vendor claim**, not an independent benchmark.  
Source: https://brave.com/search/api/

- Google says Search includes **maps**, **local businesses**, and other direct-answer features when appropriate, and Google’s AI search features provide linked summaries. Google also says **AI responses may include mistakes** and advises checking important information in more than one place.  
Sources: https://www.google.com/intl/en_us/search/howsearchworks/features/ , https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/14901683?co=GENIE.Platform%3DAndroid&hl=en , https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/16011537?co=GENIE.Platform%3DAndroid&hl=en

- For some research tasks, people use **specialized search systems** instead of a general Web engine: Google Scholar says it searches **scholarly literature** across disciplines, and PubMed says it supports search and retrieval of **biomedical and life-sciences literature** and contains **more than 40 million citations and abstracts**.  
Sources: https://scholar.google.com/intl/en/scholar/about.html , https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/about/

**Disagreement in the evidence**

- A representative-query study found **Google outperformed Bing** overall, but the gap on **informational queries** was “rather low”; on **navigational queries**, Google found the correct answer in **95.3%** of cases versus **76.6%** for Bing.  
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.2210

- Another study using **40 search terms** across **10 categories** ranked **Google first** and **Bing second** on its combined indicator.  
Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/366121641_Proposing_a_New_Combined_Indicator_for_Measuring_Search_Engine_Performance_and_Evaluating_Google_Yahoo_DuckDuckGo_and_Bing_Search_Engines_based_on_Combined_Indicator

- A 2025 coding-advice study using **1,467 Python queries** found **Bing performed best** for that domain under its Stack-Overflow-based quality proxy, and concluded coding-search quality was higher on Bing than on Google or Apple Search.  
Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.03793

- A similarity study on **300 queries** found **Google stands apart**, while **Bing and DuckDuckGo are largely indistinguishable** from each other.  
Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.00650

- A personalization study found cookie-based personalization of first-page results was about **37% for Google** and about **20% for DuckDuckGo**, and the overlap between Google and DuckDuckGo results was only about **2% to 8%** depending on category and condition.  
Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-26438-2_39

**Inference**

Because the literature says evaluation depends on **task, domain, and intent**, and because the studies above produce **different winners under different metrics**, the evidence supports a **trade-off view**, not a universal winner.  
Sources: https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/widm.1541 , https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-37688-7_9 , https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.2210 , https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.03793

If you force a practical answer for **general-purpose Web research**, **Google** has the strongest evidence for broad coverage, ecosystem features, and mainstream usage, but that is still **not proof** that it is best for **every** research question.  
Sources: https://gs.statcounter.com/search-engine-market-share , https://www.google.com/intl/en_us/search/howsearchworks/features/ , https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.2210

If you optimize for **privacy/independence**, **Brave** and **DuckDuckGo** have stronger privacy positioning, but I did **not** find equally strong independent evidence that either is best on broad research quality across all question types.  
Sources: https://brave.com/search/api/ , https://duckduckgo.com/duckduckgo-help-pages/results/sources

**Uncertainty / lack of good evidence**

- I did **not** find a credible benchmark covering **every query type, every language, every geography, every domain, and every success metric** across today’s major search engines. The sources I found all used **specific query samples**, **specific domains**, or **specific evaluation metrics**.  
Sources: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-37688-7_9 , https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/widm.1541 , https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.2210 , https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.03793

**Bottom line**

The evidence-based answer is: **there is no objectively best Web search engine for every kind of research question today**. The defensible choice depends on what you mean by “best”: **broad general Web coverage**, **privacy**, **local/commercial lookup**, **coding help**, or **scholarly/biomedical literature search**.  
Sources: https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/widm.1541 , https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-37688-7_9 , https://scholar.google.com/intl/en/scholar/about.html , https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/about/
